statement: Spacecraft 012 was undergoing a "Plugs Out Integrated Test" (procedure OCP FO-K-0021-1) at the time of the accident on 27 January 1967.

excerpt: Spacecraft 012 was undergoing a "Plugs Out Integrated Test" at the time of the accident on January 27, 1967.

statement: Spacecraft 012 was mated to the launch vehicle at Launch Complex 34 on 6 January 1967.

statement: Crew positions: Grissom was command pilot (left seat), White senior pilot (middle seat), Chaffee pilot (right seat).
locator: Part III, Interim report, Seamans to Webb, 3 Feb 1967, p. 3-49
excerpt: Lt. Colonel Grissom was the command pilot, sitting in the left seat; Lt. Colonel White, the senior pilot, sitting in the middle seat; and Lt. Commander Chaffee, the pilot, was in the right seat.

statement: Test objectives included verifying spacecraft function with all umbilicals and GSE disconnected and verifying unaided astronaut emergency egress at the end of the test.
excerpt: To verify astronaut emergency egress procedures (unaided egress) at the conclusion of the test.

statement: The Plugs-Out Test had not been classified as hazardous; only tests involving fueled vehicles, hypergolics, cryogenics, high-pressure tanks, live pyrotechnics or altitude chamber tests were routinely so classified.
excerpt: This Plugs-Out Test had not been classified as hazardous because only those tests involving fueled vehicles, hypergolic propellants, cryogenic systems, high pressure tanks, live pyrotechnics or altitude chamber tests were routinely classified as hazardous.

statement: The test was conducted with a 16.7 psia, 100-percent oxygen cabin atmosphere; the Board determined the test conditions were extremely hazardous.
locator: Part VI, Finding 2b and Determination, p. 6-1
excerpt: The test was conducted with a 16.7 pounds per square inch absolute, 100-percent oxygen atmosphere. DETERMINATION: The test conditions were extremely hazardous.

timeBasis: Source states GMT; GMT taken as equal to UTC (1967). Equivalent EST = UTC-5.

timeBasis: Source states GMT; GMT taken as equal to UTC (1967). Equivalent EST = UTC-5.

statement: Finding 1a: there was a momentary power failure at 23:30:55 GMT.

statement: All transmission of voice and data from the spacecraft terminated by 23:31:22.4 GMT, three seconds after rupture.

excerpt: It is estimated that consciousness was lost between 15 and 30 seconds after the first suit failed.

excerpt: Death of the crew was from asphyxia due to inhalation of toxic gases due to fire. A contributory cause of death was thermal burns.

excerpt: The loss of telemetry data at 23:31:22.4 GMT during the second phase of the fire makes determination of precise times of subsequent occurrences impossible.

excerpt: it is concluded that all hatches were opened and the two outer hatches removed approximately five minutes after the report of fire or at about 23:36 GMT.
timeBasis: Source states GMT; GMT taken as equal to UTC (1967). Equivalent EST = UTC-5. Minute precision only.

statement: Medical opinion based on autopsy concluded resuscitation was impossible by 23:36 GMT.
excerpt: Medical opinion, based on autopsy reports, has concluded that chances of resuscitation decreased rapidly once consciousness was lost and that resuscitation was impossible by 23:36 GMT.
timeBasis: Source states GMT; GMT taken as equal to UTC (1967). Equivalent EST = UTC-5.

statement: The doctors estimated their arrival at the White Room at 23:45 GMT; medical support was reported available at about 23:43 GMT.
excerpt: The doctors estimate their arrival to have been at 23:45 GMT.
timeBasis: Source states GMT; GMT taken as equal to UTC (1967). Equivalent EST = UTC-5.

statement: In the first stage, flames travelled along the Raschel net debris traps and Velcro strips near the ignition point also burned.
excerpt: flames moved rapidly from the point of ignition, traveling along the Raschel net debris traps which were installed in the Command Module to prevent items from dropping into equipment areas during tests or flight. At the same time, Velcro strips positioned near the ignition point also burned.

statement: Finding 2a: the Command Module contained many types and classes of combustible material contiguous to possible ignition sources; recommendation: amount and location of combustibles must be severely restricted and controlled.
locator: Part VI, Finding 2a and Recommendation (= A1-S01 p. 6-1)
excerpt: The Command Module contained many types and classes of combustible material in areas contiguous to possible ignition sources.

statement: Panel 5 notes that polyurethane foam and nylon netting lay close to where arcs would occur if the Teflon insulation of the chafed bundle were defeated.
excerpt: Combustibles in the fonn of polyurethane foam and nylon netting lay close to the electrical arcs and sparks that would occur if the Teflon insulation were defeated.
notes: Excerpt reproduces OCR text including the OCR error "fonn" (form).

statement: The Senate committee found combustible-material standards too low, no criteria for placement of material to limit propagation, and nonflight materials present at the time of the fire.
excerpt: there were nonflight materials inside the spacecraft.

statement: The Board concluded the fire was most probably brought about by some minor malfunction or failure of equipment or wire insulation, which most likely will never be positively identified.
excerpt: The fire in Apollo 204 was most probably brought about by some minor malfunction or failure of equipment or wire insulation. This failure, which most likely will never be positively identified, initiated a sequence of events that culminated in the conflagration.

statement: Finding 1c: no single ignition source of the fire was conclusively identified.
excerpt: No single ignition source of the fire was conclusively identified.
notes: Central distinction: the exact ignition source is unproven; the arc determination below is a "most probable" judgement.

statement: Determination 1: the most probable initiator was an electrical arc in the -Y/+Z sector, best fitting near the floor in the lower forward left-hand equipment bay where ECS instrumentation power wiring leads between the ECU and the oxygen panel.
excerpt: The most probable initiator was an electrical arc in the sector between the -Y and +Z spacecraft axes. The exact location best fitting the total available information is near the floor in the lower forward section of the left-hand equipment bay
notes: Exact PDF wording; the NASA web transcription (A1-S02) omits "the" before -Y.

statement: Fire-damage patterns indicate the most likely start region is beneath the lithium hydroxide access door, where power cable insulation was vulnerable to abrasion by the door edge, but this cannot be proven because cable and door edge were destroyed.
locator: Part V §4c "Electric Arcs" (= A1-S01 p. 5-10, as corrected by Appendix G Part 1 erratum 26)
excerpt: If this cable were the cause, it cannot be proven since both the power cable and the inside edge of the door were completely destroyed.
notes: The scanned PDF misprints "lighium hydroxide"; Appendix G Part 1 erratum 26 corrects it.

statement: The Board judged it most probable that an electric arc started the fire either under the LiOH access door or elsewhere near the ECU; other powered ECU cables may have been the source but destruction precludes positive determination.
excerpt: It is most probable that the fire was initiated by an electric arc either in this location or in some other region near the Environmental Control Unit.

statement: The time of initiation probably coincides with the spacecraft power interruption at 23:30:55 GMT.
excerpt: The time of initiation probably coincides with the spacecraft power interruption at 23:30:55 GMT.
timeBasis: Source states GMT; GMT taken as equal to UTC (1967). Equivalent EST = UTC-5.
notes: Probable, not established; the Board also cautions that the pre-fire data transients may be effects rather than causes of the fire.

statement: Of several arc craters found near power cables, only one appeared closely linked in time to the fire, and full investigation relegated it to a low probability.
excerpt: A complete investigation of the evidence associated with this possible ignition source has relegated it to a low probability.
notes: Alternative candidate arc considered and down-weighted by the Board.

statement: The Board cautioned that the pre-fire data transients and crew activity may as easily be associated with the result of the fire as with its cause.
excerpt: It should be noted that these data transients and subsequent activity of the crew may as easily be associated with the result of the fire as with the cause.

statement: Electrostatic discharge, spontaneous combustion, mechanically produced heat and struck-object impact were eliminated as reasonable ignition possibilities; flowing-oxygen energy was also eliminated.
excerpt: Electrostatic discharge, spontaneous combustion of flammable material, mechanically produced heat by machinery and heat from the impact of a struck object have been eliminated as reasonable possibilities of ignition of the fire.

statement: The Board concluded none of the electrically powered spacecraft systems or subassemblies was associated with initiating the fire.
excerpt: The results of this effort led to the conclusion that none of the electrically powered spacecraft systems or subassemblies was associated with the initiation of the fire.

statement: There was no substantial evidence that water/glycol coolant was involved in initiating the fire, although spilled coolant on damaged wiring can provide fuel and ignition mechanism (shown in laboratory tests).
excerpt: There is no substantial evidence that coolant was involved in the initiation of the fire.

statement: No evidence was discovered that suggested sabotage.
excerpt: No evidence was discovered that suggested sabotage.
notes: Panel 5 Finding 8 (A1-S03 p. D-5-15) reaches the same determination after searching for unaccounted objects.

statement: Panel 5: no arc could be positively identified as the unique ignition source; three arcs had all elements needed to cause the disaster, two showing poor engineering and installation.
locator: Section D, Finding 9 Determination, p. D-5-15
excerpt: No arc could be positively identified as the unique ignItIon source. Three were found that l}ad, all of the elements needed to cause the disaster. Two of these showed evidence of poor engineering and installation.
notes: Excerpt reproduces OCR artifacts ("ignItIon", "l}ad,").

statement: Panel 5 identified two candidate regions: arcing in the extreme lower-left corner of the Lower Equipment Bay (cover of junction box C-15-1A-52) and in the right-hand portion of the Left-Hand Equipment Bay; each "could have provided" a primary ignition source.
locator: Section D, Findings 3 and 4 Determinations, p. D-5-14
excerpt: Electrical arcing in the extreme lower left hand corner of this bay could have provided a primary ignition source.
notes: Panel 5 keeps more than one candidate open; the Board's Determination 1 narrows to the left-hand equipment bay near the ECU/oxygen panel. Not a direct conflict, but a difference in specificity.

statement: Panel 5 described a wire bundle over a waste-management tube below the ECU CO2/odor absorber access door whose lower edge may have chafed the unguarded Teflon insulation.
excerpt: When the door was opened and closed, its lower . edge may have chafed the wires of this bundle .
notes: Hypothesis ("may have"); not proven.

statement: Panel 5 found the arc at the C-15-1A-52 cover plate could not be eliminated as a primary ignition source (possibly via glycol residue igniting Velcro), and called for experiments.
excerpt: Therefore, based on this possibility the arcing in the above area cannot be eliminated as a possible primary ignition source.

statement: Whether a short occurred in the ECU instrumentation power-supply harness cannot be determined because the lingering fire destroyed the bundle.
excerpt: Whether or not a short occurred cannot be detennined because of extensive destruction of the wire bundle by the lingering fire in this area.
notes: Notably, this is the ECS instrumentation power wiring named in Board Determination 1.

statement: A full-scale boilerplate mock-up fire, ignited by a hot wire in the suspected area, closely reproduced the total fire time and pressure history.
excerpt: Total time of the fire and the pressure history reproduced those of the fire quite closely thus adding confidence to the deduced origin and mode of propagation of the fire.

statement: Three hatches were installed: the boost protective cover (BPC) hatch, the middle ablative hatch and the inner pressure-vessel hatch.
excerpt: Three hatches were installed on the Command Module.

excerpt: With a slightly higher pressure inside the Command Module than outside, opening the inner hatch is impossible because of the resulting force on the hatch.

statement: Finding 4: due to internal pressure the inner hatch could not be opened prior to rupture; the crew was never capable of effecting emergency egress. Recommendation: reduce egress time and simplify egress operations.
locator: Part VI, Finding 4, Determination and Recommendation, p. 6-1
excerpt: The crew was never capable of effecting emergency egress because of the pressurization before rupture and their loss of consciousness soon after rupture.

statement: Opening the cabin vent valve would have delayed rupture by less than one second, as venting capacity was insufficient.
excerpt: It is estimated that opening the valve would have delayed Command Module rupture by less than one second.

statement: The Senate committee states the inward-opening hatch required at least 90 seconds for removal and crew egress, and the 16.7 psi atmosphere plus fire pressure prevented opening without depressurization.
notes: Text read in OCR ("equipped with an inward openino- hatch wh1ch required at least 90 seconds"); excerpt withheld because of OCR corruption.

statement: The Senate committee reports NASA had weighed a quick-opening hatch and judged the risk of accidental release in space to exceed its benefits.
excerpt: the possibility of accidental release in space of a quick-opening hatch (like the ones used in the earlier spacecraft) was considered to impose a risk in excess of the benefits to be gained from such a hatch.
notes: Contemporary design trade-off (decision made before the accident).

statement: Borman testified that a hatch opening outward in 2 seconds would have let the crew escape, and that in his firm opinion they would have escaped with one opening in 8 seconds.

notes: Read in a heavily corrupted OCR layer; excerpt withheld. Retrospective opinion of a Board member, not a Board finding.

statement: Finding 5: organizations responsible failed to identify the test as hazardous; no contingency preparations for escape or rescue from an internal CM fire; emergency fire, rescue and medical teams were not in attendance.
excerpt: Those organizations responsible for the planning, conduct and safety of this test failed to identify it as being hazardous.

statement: Determination 5: adequate safety precautions were neither established nor observed for this test.
excerpt: Adequate safety precautions were neither established nor observed for this test.

statement: Recommendations 5: management continually monitor test safety; review emergency equipment; regular emergency training; modify service structures and umbilical towers.
excerpt: Service structures and umbilical towers be modified to facilitate emergency operations.

statement: Finding 9: the ECS design provides a pure oxygen atmosphere, a severe fire hazard unless combustibles are restricted; recommended full-scale mock-up fire testing and continued diluent-gas studies.
excerpt: This atmosphere presents severe fire hazards if the amount and location of combustibles in the Command Module are not restricted and controlled.

excerpt: These deficiencies created an unnecessarily hazardous condition and their continuation would imperil any future Apollo operations.

statement: Recommendations 10 include ECS review, stronger plumbing joints, eliminating coolant-leak effects, 3-D jigs and rigid wiring inspection, vibration tests, no powered connect/disconnect, fire extinguishing means and auxiliary breathing oxygen.

statement: The Board found numerous examples of poor wiring installation, design and workmanship (e.g. a wrench socket found in the spacecraft); Teflon insulation was vulnerable to abrasion and cold flow.

statement: Determination 11: problems of program management and relationships between Centers and with the contractor led in some cases to insufficient response to changing requirements.
excerpt: Problems of program management and relationships between Centers and with the contractor have led in some cases to insufficient response to changing program requirements.

statement: The Board summarized six conditions that led to the disaster: sealed oxygen cabin, extensive combustibles, vulnerable wiring, vulnerable coolant plumbing, inadequate escape provisions, inadequate rescue/medical provisions.
excerpt: Although the Board was not able to determine conclusively the specific initiator of the Apollo 204 fire, it has identified the conditions which led to the disaster.

statement: The Board concluded the Apollo team failed to give adequate attention to mundane but vital crew-safety questions, revealing many deficiencies in design, engineering, manufacture and quality control.

statement: Hatch-opening time for the new hatch differs: Chariots says it would open outward in five seconds; the Apollo 7 press kit says seven seconds from inside and 10 seconds by a pad crew.
locator: Section "Spacecraft Design Changes, Materials Substitution" (PDF p. 43)
excerpt: The new aluminum and fiberglas hatch can be opened from inSide in seven seconds and by a pad safety crew in 10 seconds.
notes: Compare A1-S05 p. 228. Excerpt reproduces OCR "inSide".

statement: House Subcommittee on NASA Oversight report: the subcommittee's own report on the accident could not be located or retrieved; only a hearing excerpt (A1-S09) was read.
